vignette:
At twenty-one, she is one of the youngest nurses on her ward, quick with her hands and careful with her voice. She grew up on an island in Oceania where most people know one another’s families, and where service is spoken about as both duty and inheritance. When she talks about why she enlisted, she does not make it dramatic. She says she wanted training, steady pay, and a way to do something useful. Nursing felt practical. She had always been the one in her family who stayed calm when someone was injured, the one who could clean a cut or sit beside a sick relative through the night. Before deployment, she imagines the work will be difficult but meaningful. She thinks of bandages, triage, long shifts, and being tired in an honest way.

The event she returns to most often begins in heat, dust, and noise. She is deployed with a medical unit in a combat zone and has already seen injuries that shock her at first and then become, if not normal, at least survivable to witness. She tells herself she can manage as long as she keeps moving. One afternoon, incoming fire hits near the treatment area. She remembers the impact more in fragments than in sequence: the violent crack, the metal rattle, someone shouting for cover, then the sudden flood of casualties. The place where she had been sorting supplies moments earlier is torn open. She drops low, then gets up because people are screaming and training takes over before fear fully lands.

She works on a wounded soldier whose blood soaks through her gloves faster than she can replace them. Another medic beside her is shouting instructions, but the words come as if through water. There is smoke, grit in her mouth, and the sour smell of explosives mixed with burned fabric and flesh. At some point she realizes one of the men brought in is someone she knows well enough to have shared jokes with at breakfast that morning. His face is altered enough that she hesitates for half a second before recognizing him. That hesitation is what she cannot forgive in herself. In her memory, it stretches into a moral failure. She remembers pressing down on a wound, hearing herself say “stay with me,” and already knowing from the look in his eyes that he is slipping away. The attack continues in bursts, and she keeps working while terrified that the next hit will land directly on them.

Afterward, she does what everyone around her does. She cleans up. She restocks. She answers questions in short, efficient phrases. She does not cry until much later, alone, and even then it feels less like crying than like her body forcing something through her. She sleeps lightly after that, boots on, uniform half-zipped, waking at every metallic sound. During the rest of deployment, she becomes sharper and more distant at once. She scans rooftops and road edges automatically. She startles when someone comes up behind her. When helicopters pass overhead, her shoulders rise before she can stop them. She stops writing home about what her days are like and fills messages with harmless details about weather and meals.

Back home, people tell her she is safe now, and she understands that intellectually. Her body does not seem to believe it. On the ward where she works now, the ordinary sounds of hospital life can abruptly pull her backward. A dropped instrument, a monitor alarm, the smell of cautery, a patient shouting from pain—all of it can tilt the room. For a moment she is no longer in the present hospital but back in the treatment area overseas, heart pounding, hands cold, eyes searching for the source of attack. She recovers quickly on the outside. Colleagues see her pause, take a breath, and continue hanging fluids or checking observations. Inside, she feels as if she has just outrun something lethal.

At night she has the same dream in different forms. In it she is trying to reach someone she knows, but the floor lengthens, her gloves tear, or no sound comes out when she calls for help. She wakes soaked in sweat, already sitting upright, sometimes grabbing at her bedsheets as if they are field dressings. Her partner has learned not to touch her suddenly when she wakes because she once swung an arm at him before she was fully conscious, then cried from shame when she realized where she was. She apologizes often, for things that do not require apology.

She avoids crowded bars, fireworks, action movies, and news clips from conflict zones. She takes the long way into work if road repairs make traffic bunch up too tightly. In supermarkets she chooses the aisle closest to the exit. She tells herself these are preferences, not fear. But her world has narrowed. She used to meet friends easily, laugh loudly, stay out late. Now she makes excuses and goes home early, exhausted by the effort of appearing normal.

The hardest part for her is the guilt. She replays that day with relentless precision, searching for the second when she might have done more, moved faster, chosen differently. As a nurse, she is praised for being capable under pressure, and that praise lands awkwardly. She thinks of all the people she could not keep alive. When patients on her current ward deteriorate unexpectedly, she feels a surge of panic and anger at herself out of proportion to the moment. She knows she is competent. She also feels, deep down, that she failed where it mattered most.

In sessions, she speaks steadily, but her hands knot in her lap whenever she gets close to the memory. She says she wants to feel like she has come home. Instead, she moves through the present as though danger is only briefly out of sight.
